conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re not carrying the weight of new motherhood alone. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after birth, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me otherwise or there’s an immediate safety concern. We’ll go one question at a time; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll keep it conversational. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[sighs, eyes on lap]  
I’ve tried… I’ll smile when my partner jokes or when the baby makes a funny face, but the laughter just feels… flat, like it doesn’t reach me inside. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to really find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
Not really… I mean, I can force a little chuckle if someone else is laughing, but it doesn’t come naturally anymore. Nothing feels truly funny these days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]  
I keep thinking I *should* look forward to stuff—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the moment comes, it just feels… blah. I go through the motions, but that excited feeling never really shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes sting, voice cracks]  
Yeah… pretty much every time she fusses for more than a few minutes I think, "What am I doing wrong?" Yesterday she wouldn’t nap and I ended up crying in the rocker, convinced it’s because I’m not good at reading her cues. I know it’s probably normal baby stuff, but my brain keeps saying it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
All the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds weird, or I’ll lie awake picturing her crib sheet bunching up around her face. Nothing actually happens, but the thoughts just flood in and I can’t shut them off. Even when my partner says everything’s fine, my stomach stays tight like something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[exhales shakily]  
Yeah… it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was just folding her tiny onesies and suddenly my heart was racing and I felt I couldn’t catch my breath. There wasn’t any real danger, but for a minute I was sure something awful was about to happen. It passes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

[shoulders sag]  
Most days, yeah. It feels like the moment I finish one feeding, the next is already due, plus the laundry and bottles… it just piles up. I’ll sit down for a second and remember five other things I haven’t done, and my chest gets tight. I keep telling myself to push through, but it’s like I’m always one step behind and sinking.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly, eyes rimmed red]  
That’s been the worst part. I finally get her down, but the second my head hits the pillow my mind starts racing—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she breathing, will she wake up in ten minutes? I lie there staring at the ceiling for hours. Even when I do drift off, every tiny squeak from the bassinet jolts me awake. I’m exhausted, but sleep just won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice small]  
Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I see other moms posting happy pictures and I think, “Why can’t I feel that way?” I end up crying in the shower so no one sees. It’s not just being tired—it’s this deep, aching sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses a tissue to her eyes]  
Yeah... it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Sometimes it’s when she won’t settle and I feel useless, other times it’s nothing specific—just this wave of misery that makes me put her in the crib real quick so I can go sob in the bathroom. I tell myself I should be happy she’s healthy, but the tears just come anyway.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes wide]  
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

I hear how heavy each day feels right now: the laughter that won't quite reach your heart, the constant knot of worry that something might happen to your baby, and the deep tiredness that sleep doesn't fix. You're working so hard to meet your little one's needs while judging yourself harshly for every hiccup, and it makes sense that you feel stuck under a cloud that won't lift.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh naturally and finds nothing funny anymore, aligning with "Not at all".</sym>, <sym>"Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "pretty much every time" and attributes baby's fussing to personal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries without cause (breathing, crib sheet) that she 'can't shut off,' matching 'Yes, very often.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness) occurring frequently ('out of nowhere', 'yesterday'), matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent daily struggles with managing tasks and feeling overwhelmed, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, hours of lying awake, and repeated awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with uncontrollable crying and inability to feel joy, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying 3-4 times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. Patient describes two weeks of <sym>daily sadness</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym> (<quote>nothing feels truly funny</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym> (<quote>it's my fault</quote>), <sym>panic symptoms</sym> (<quote>heart racing...can't catch my breath</quote>), and <sym>middle-of-night worry</sym> despite infant sleep opportunities, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. <sym>Anxious features</sym> are prominent; no suicidal ideation (Q10=0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetric or primary care provider</med> to review results and consider therapy and/or medication
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for formal diagnostic evaluation and evidence-based therapy (CBT or IPT)
3. Encourage 15-20 min outdoor daylight walks and acceptance of help with night feeds to improve <sym>sleep hygiene</sym>
4. Provide 24/7 hotlines: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773 and National Maternal Mental Health line 1-833-943-5746
5. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to track progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: ___  
Screener: ___  

1. Symptom Endorsements  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
- Marked generalized and “what-if” anxiety, panic episodes without clear trigger (Q4, 5)  
- Subjective “overwhelm,” sense of falling behind in daily tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia despite infant sleep opportunities (Q7)  

2. Pattern Consistency  
All responses converge on moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms plus significant comorbid anxiety; no current suicidal ideation (Q10 denied).

3. Flagged Risk Factors  
- Daily sadness and crying > 2 weeks  
- Loss of interest / pleasure in formerly enjoyable activities  
- Self-attribution of infant difficulties as maternal failure  
- Recurrent intrusive catastrophic thoughts about infant safety  
- Panic-type episodes (heart racing, breathlessness) occurring spontaneously  
- Chronic sleep deprivation secondary to worry, compounding fatigue and mood lability  

4. Safety  
Denies any thoughts of self-harm or desire to be away from baby; no protective concerns voiced.

5. Screening Impression  
Findings exceed cut-off for probable Major Depressive Episode with anxious features in the postpartum period; meet threshold for urgent referral to obstetric/primary provider and mental health specialty for formal diagnostic evaluation and treatment discussion.

Next Step: Discuss results with patient; facilitate same-day warm-handoff or scheduled appointment for comprehensive assessment.
